lrs-s-whitman.summary: Clean Air Act § 109(b) unambiguously bars EPA from considering implementation costs when setting national ambient air quality standards; the instruction to set standards “requisite” to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety is an intelligible principle, and an agency cannot cure an unconstitutional delegation by limiting its own discretion.

sections.Parties: Christine Todd Whitman, Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, and the EPA represented the federal government; the challenged standards were issued in 1997, before she took office. American Trucking Associations and other companies and organizations, together with Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia, challenged the standards, arguing that EPA’s reading gave it excessive discretion and that the statute should let it weigh compliance costs. The government’s petition (No. 99-1257) and the challengers’ cross-petition (No. 99-1426) were decided together.
sections.Material Facts: Under § 108 of the Clean Air Act EPA identifies covered pollutants and issues air quality criteria; under § 109 it sets national ambient air quality standards which states implement through plans under § 110. Section 109(b)(1) requires primary standards that, in the Administrator’s judgment, based on the criteria and allowing an adequate margin of safety, are requisite to protect public health. On July 18, 1997 EPA revised the ozone and particulate-matter standards, moving ozone from a one-hour to an eight-hour measure without considering compliance costs. A second dispute concerned implementation: Subpart 1 of Part D states general requirements for nonattainment areas, while Subpart 2, added in 1990, classifies ozone areas by severity. In the rule’s preamble EPA announced that it would implement the new standard under Subpart 1, keeping Subpart 2 for the old standard only until an area attained it.
sections.Procedural History: The challengers sought direct review in the D.C. Circuit under § 307(b)(1), 42 U.S.C. § 7607(b)(1), review of rulemaking rather than an appeal from a trial. The panel, 175 F.3d 1027 (1999), with a further decision on rehearing at 195 F.3d 4, held that EPA had construed § 109 to confer discretion without an intelligible principle but, instead of invalidating the statute, remanded so EPA could adopt a limiting construction; Judge Tatel dissented on that point. The panel unanimously rejected consideration of costs, recognized EPA’s power to revise the ozone standard, held that Subpart 2 constrained implementation of a revised standard, and on rehearing treated EPA’s implementation interpretation as final agency action. The Supreme Court granted both petitions, heard argument on November 7, 2000, and decided the case on February 27, 2001, affirming in part, reversing in part and remanding.
sections.Issue: Does § 109(b) permit EPA to consider implementation costs when setting the level requisite to protect public health or welfare? If costs are excluded, does the statute supply an intelligible principle, or does it unconstitutionally delegate legislative power, and can an agency cure such a delegation by restricting its own authority? Separately, was EPA’s announced interpretation of the ozone implementation provisions final and ripe for review, and was it a permissible reading of Subparts 1 and 2?
sections.Holding: Justice Scalia wrote the principal opinion; Parts I and IV were unanimous, all but Breyer joined Part II on costs, and all but Stevens and Souter joined Part III on delegation. Section 109(b) unambiguously excludes implementation costs from the setting of national standards, primary and secondary; the Court did not hold costs irrelevant elsewhere in the Act. Section 109(b)(1) supplies an intelligible principle: standards sufficient, but not more than necessary, to protect public health with an adequate margin of safety, and the Constitution does not require Congress to specify a numerical concentration. An agency’s voluntary self-limitation cannot cure a delegation that lacks a constitutionally adequate standard. EPA’s implementation interpretation was final and ripe, but it could not lawfully read the Act to let Subpart 2’s ozone-specific restrictions largely disappear; the agency was left to find a permissible construction on remand.
sections.Reasoning: Section 109(b)(1) directs EPA to determine what is requisite to protect public health on the basis of scientific criteria; nothing in that instruction tells the agency to weigh health against the cost. Elsewhere Congress expressly mentioned costs and economic feasibility and repeatedly revised the Act without adding such language to § 109; a change of that magnitude cannot hide in terms like “judgment” or “adequate margin,” for Congress does not hide elephants in mouseholes. On delegation, under J. W. Hampton a statute must supply an intelligible principle; the D.C. Circuit’s remedy inverted the inquiry, because an agency choosing how much discretion to exercise would itself make the policy decision the doctrine reserves to Congress. Section 109 identified the task, the evidence, the protected interest and the degree of protection, and it fell comfortably within delegations upheld in Touby, unlike the 1935 statutes struck down in Panama Refining and Schechter. The implementation ruling was final because the preamble stated a considered position; under the then-governing Chevron framework the subparts’ interaction was ambiguous, but EPA’s reading would strip Congress’s detailed ozone restrictions of their force.

lrs-s-whitman.separateOpinions: Justice Thomas joined the opinion but questioned whether the intelligible-principle test fully enforces Article I, suggesting that some decisions may be too important to delegate even with a principle. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, agreed the statute was constitutional but would call the delegated power legislative and hold that Congress may delegate it within adequate limits. Justice Breyer agreed costs were excluded here because the Act’s technology-forcing design, structure and history showed it, but would not read regulatory silence generally as forbidding attention to serious adverse consequences. Loper Bright (2024) later overruled Chevron but preserved stare decisis for prior holdings on specific agency actions.

lrs-s-gundy.summary: A fractured Court upheld SORNA’s grant to the Attorney General of authority to specify the statute’s application to pre-Act offenders: Kagan’s four-Justice plurality read the Act to require registration of pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving only transitional details, while Alito concurred in the judgment under existing doctrine and Gorsuch, Roberts and Thomas would have held the delegation unconstitutional.

sections.Parties: Herman Avery Gundy was the criminal defendant in the Southern District of New York, the appellant in the Second Circuit and the petitioner in the Supreme Court. The United States prosecuted him for failing to register under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) and defended his conviction. Gundy argued that Congress unconstitutionally delegated legislative power when it authorized the Attorney General to specify SORNA’s applicability to people convicted before the Act.
sections.Material Facts: Section 20913(a) requires an offender to register and keep the registration current where he lives, works or studies; § 20913(b) sets the initial deadline, before release from prison or within three business days of a nonprison sentence. Section 20913(d), the challenged provision, authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of the requirements to offenders convicted before enactment. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2250(a) a registrant who travels interstate and knowingly fails to register faces up to ten years in prison. The Attorney General issued an interim rule in February 2007 and a final rule in December 2010 applying SORNA to all pre-Act offenders. Gundy had pleaded guilty in Maryland in 2005 to a sexual offense involving a minor. While serving a later federal sentence he traveled by bus from Pennsylvania to a Bronx reentry center on July 17, 2012 and never registered in Maryland or New York.
sections.Procedural History: The district court first dismissed the indictment, but the Second Circuit reinstated it, holding that Gundy was required to register no later than August 1, 2008, 804 F.3d 140 (2015). After a bench trial on stipulated facts the district court found the elements proved and on June 16, 2016 sentenced him to time served and five years of supervised release. The Second Circuit affirmed on June 22, 2017, 695 F. App’x 639, rejecting the nondelegation argument as foreclosed by circuit precedent. The Supreme Court granted certiorari on the nondelegation question only, heard argument on October 2, 2018, and affirmed on June 20, 2019. Justice Kagan announced the judgment for a plurality (Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor); Justice Alito concurred in the judgment; Justice Gorsuch dissented with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas; Justice Kavanaugh did not participate.
sections.Issue: Does Congress violate Article I’s vesting of legislative power when it authorizes the Attorney General to specify the applicability of SORNA’s registration requirements to offenders convicted before the statute’s enactment? Read with the rest of SORNA, does § 20913(d) require registration of all pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, leaving transitional decisions, or does it let the Attorney General decide whether, when and to what extent they are covered at all?
sections.Holding: The Court affirmed the conviction 5–3. The plurality held that the scope of a delegation must be fixed by statutory interpretation before its constitutionality is assessed, construed SORNA to require the Attorney General to apply the registration requirements to pre-Act offenders as soon as feasible, and held that this limited assignment easily satisfied the intelligible-principle test; the words “as soon as feasible” are the plurality’s construction, not statutory text. Alito supplied the fifth vote because he could not say the statute lacked a discernible standard under existing doctrine, but he joined neither Kagan’s reading nor her reasoning. Neither the plurality’s analysis nor the dissent’s proposed test is a five-Justice holding.
sections.Reasoning: Kagan began with the relationship between interpretation and nondelegation: a court cannot judge the adequacy of Congress’s instructions until it knows what authority the statute confers. Reynolds v. United States had held that SORNA did not apply to pre-Act offenders until the Attorney General acted, but the plurality read Reynolds as recognizing only a practical reason for delay: the need to bring a large existing population into the system. The declaration of purpose announced a comprehensive national system, § 20913(d)’s pairing with rulemaking authority for offenders unable to comply with subsection (b) marked it as a transition provision. So read, the Attorney General could weigh administrative difficulties but could not decline indefinitely to register pre-Act offenders; the limit came from the statute, not from the official’s restraint. Gorsuch, dissenting, tied nondelegation to bicameralism, presentment and accountability, and would allow Congress only to let others fill in details after fixing policy, make a rule contingent on executive fact-finding, or assign nonlegislative duties; SORNA fit none, because deciding which pre-Act offenders face criminally enforceable duties is the coverage choice itself.

lrs-s-gundy.separateOpinions: Justice Alito, concurring in the judgment, agreed that Congress may not transfer legislative power but observed that since 1935 the Court had upheld very broad delegations under capacious standards; he would support reconsidering the doctrine if a majority were willing, but would not single out this statute under a newly demanding approach. Justice Gorsuch, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, would have held the delegation unconstitutional. FCC v. Consumers’ Research (2025) later applied the intelligible-principle framework and upheld the universal-service delegation, Kagan writing for six Justices including Roberts, Kavanaugh and Barrett.

lrs-s-chadha.summary: Congress can alter the legal rights, duties and relations of persons outside the legislative branch only by passing a bill through both Houses and presenting it to the President, so the one-House veto of the Attorney General’s suspension of a deportation was unconstitutional; the veto was severable, leaving the suspension power intact.

sections.Parties: Jagdish Rai Chadha, of East Indian origin, born in Kenya and holding a British passport, was the person ordered deported; he petitioned the Ninth Circuit and was an appellee and respondent in the Supreme Court. The Immigration and Naturalization Service, which administered the statute for the Attorney General, was the appellant even though it agreed with Chadha that the legislative veto was unconstitutional, because it would enforce the deportation order unless a court prevented it. The House of Representatives and the Senate defended the veto, intervened, and filed their own petitions for certiorari.
sections.Material Facts: Chadha lawfully entered the United States in 1966 on a student visa that expired on June 30, 1972, and stayed. On October 11, 1973 the INS ordered him to show cause why he should not be deported; he conceded deportability and applied under § 244(a)(1) for suspension of deportation. An immigration judge suspended his deportation on June 25, 1974 and reported it to Congress. Under § 244(c)(2) either House could, before the end of the next session, adopt a resolution disapproving the suspension, in which case the Attorney General had to deport. On December 12, 1975 Representative Eilberg introduced House Resolution 926 opposing permanent residence for six aliens, including Chadha, after his subcommittee reviewed 340 suspensions. On December 16 the House adopted it without printing, debate or a recorded vote; it went neither to the Senate nor to the President. Chadha was ordered deported on November 8, 1976.
sections.Procedural History: The immigration judge and the Board of Immigration Appeals held they had no power to decide whether § 244(c)(2) was constitutional and dismissed Chadha’s appeal. He petitioned the Ninth Circuit for review under § 106(a). The INS agreed the veto was unconstitutional, so the court invited the House and Senate to file briefs as amici. The Ninth Circuit held that the House lacked constitutional authority to order Chadha’s deportation by this mechanism and directed the Attorney General not to deport him on the basis of the resolution, 634 F.2d 408 (1980). The INS appealed under 28 U.S.C. § 1252 and both Houses petitioned for certiorari; the Court heard argument on February 22, 1982 and reargument on December 7, 1982, and affirmed on June 23, 1983. Chief Justice Burger wrote for six Justices; Justice Powell concurred in the judgment; Justice White dissented; Justice Rehnquist, joined by White, dissented on severability.
sections.Issue: May Congress authorize either House, acting alone and without presentment to the President, to overturn the Attorney General’s suspension of an individual’s deportation? Is the House’s action legislative in character, so that Article I requires bicameral passage and presentment, or may it operate as a condition reserved when Congress delegated the suspension authority? If the veto is unconstitutional, is it severable from the suspension power, and do the parties’ alignment and the possibility of other immigration relief prevent decision?
sections.Holding: Yes to jurisdiction and justiciability: the INS was aggrieved by a judgment that barred it from executing an order it would otherwise enforce; Chadha had standing and faced a concrete injury; possible alternative relief was speculative; Congress’s defense supplied adversity; and Congress’s plenary power over immigration did not make the constitutionality of its procedure a political question. On the merits, when Congress takes action that is legislative in purpose and effect it must comply with bicameralism and presentment unless the Constitution itself provides otherwise. The House resolution altered the legal rights, duties and relations of Chadha and executive officials outside the legislative branch, so § 244(c)(2)’s one-House veto was unconstitutional. The provision was severable under the Act’s severability clause, leaving the suspension power and reporting requirement in place. The Ninth Circuit was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The severability clause created a presumption that Congress did not intend the whole scheme to depend on the veto. On the merits Burger began with Article I, §§ 1 and 7: legislative power is vested in a Congress of two Houses, bills must pass both and be presented to the President, and § 7, clause 3 extends presentment to orders, resolutions and votes so that Congress cannot evade it by renaming its action. The resolution was legislative in character because of what it did: it overruled the Attorney General’s decision and imposed a duty to deport; once Congress delegated the authority it had to respect the delegation until it legislated again. The Attorney General’s own action differed because it was taken under an enacted law and reviewable for conformity to it. The Constitution names four situations in which one House acts alone with binding effect (impeachment, impeachment trial, appointments, treaties), and this was not among them. Nearly two hundred statutes had used legislative vetoes, but efficiency and convenience cannot save a procedure contrary to the Constitution.

lrs-s-chadha.separateOpinions: Justice Powell concurred in the judgment on a narrower ground: by deciding that six named individuals failed the statutory hardship criteria, the House assumed a judicial function without the safeguards of a hearing or an impartial tribunal. Justice White dissented, defending the legislative veto as an accommodation between broad delegation and congressional responsibility: agency rules also change legal rights without passing both Houses, and the veto was a condition built into an Article I statute, so a permanent change in Chadha’s status required the functional agreement of the Executive, House and Senate. Justice Rehnquist, joined by White, dissented on severability, because Congress had repeatedly refused to give the Executive unconditional suspension authority.

lrs-k-riggs.summary: A statute’s general words yield to the evident intention of its makers and to the common-law maxim that no one may profit from his own wrong, so a grandson who murdered the testator to secure his inheritance cannot take under a will that the wills statutes, read literally, would give effect to.

sections.Parties: The plaintiffs and appellants were Philo Riggs, as guardian ad litem, and Francis B. Palmer’s two daughters, Mrs. Riggs and Mrs. Preston, who received small legacies under the will and sought to keep the estate from passing to the murderer. The defendants and respondents were Elmer E. Palmer, the testator’s sixteen-year-old grandson and residuary legatee, and the estate’s administrator; Elmer claimed the property under a formally valid, probated will. Judge Earl wrote for the Court of Appeals of New York on October 8, 1889; Judge Gray dissented.
sections.Material Facts: On August 13, 1880 Francis Palmer made a will leaving small legacies to his daughters and the residue of his farm and considerable personal property to his grandson Elmer, subject to support for Elmer’s mother. Francis later married Mrs. Bresee under an antenuptial agreement charging her support against the farm. Elmer lived in his grandfather’s household, knew of the provisions in his favor, and knew that Francis had shown an intention to revoke them. To prevent revocation and obtain immediate possession, Elmer willfully poisoned his grandfather in 1882. He was convicted of second-degree murder and was serving his sentence in the state reformatory when this civil action began. The statutes governing the making, proof, effect and revocation of wills contained no provision disqualifying a beneficiary who murders the testator; read literally, they gave the residue to Elmer.
sections.Procedural History: The daughters sued to cancel and annul the provisions of the will in Elmer’s favor. A referee found that Elmer intentionally murdered Francis to prevent revocation of the will and accelerate his inheritance, yet concluded that the wills statutes required dismissal of the complaint; judgment was entered on the report and the General Term affirmed. On the daughters’ appeal the Court of Appeals accepted the facts found, reversed both judgments, and entered judgment enjoining Elmer and the administrator from using the estate for Elmer’s benefit, declaring the devise and bequest to him ineffective, and declaring the daughters owners of the estate subject to the support charges for Elmer’s mother and Francis’s widow.
sections.Issue: May a beneficiary acquire property under a formally valid and probated will after intentionally murdering the testator to prevent revocation and accelerate the inheritance, when the governing statutes contain no express slayer provision and, read literally, transfer the estate to him? Or may a court restrain a statute’s general words by the evident intention of the legislature and fundamental maxims of the common law?
sections.Holding: Elmer cannot take any interest in the estate. The wills statutes were enacted to carry out testators’ wishes and secure the orderly devolution of property, and a legislature pursuing those ends would never have intended a legatee who murdered the testator to benefit under the will; a case within the letter of a statute is not within the statute unless it is within the intention of its makers. Independently, all statutes and contracts are controlled by the maxim that no one shall profit by his own fraud, take advantage of his own wrong, or acquire property by his own crime. The ruling takes no property Elmer possessed and adds no punishment; it holds only that he shall not acquire property by his crime. Reversed, with judgment for the daughters.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Earl reasoned from legislative purpose, the equity of the statute and the absurdity doctrine. He conceded that the statutes, literally read, gave the property to the murderer, but held that their purpose controlled: what is within the makers’ intention is within the statute though outside its letter, and what is within the letter is outside the statute if outside the intention. Blackstone’s examples supplied the method: a law letting a man try all causes in his manor does not reach his own case. Common-law maxims against profiting from one’s own wrong were a second, independent ground, background law that governs statutes and wills unless legislation displaces it. The causal link made the maxim decisive: Francis might have revoked, and by killing him Elmer made the will speak at the time he chose. Judge Gray’s dissent applied a strictly textual method: the legislature had regulated wills with comprehensive particularity; the civil-law slayer rules supplied reasons for legislation, not judicial power, and stripping Elmer of the legacy added a penalty beyond his sentence.

lrs-k-vanderstok.summary: A weapon parts kit that ships with every part needed and can be finished in about twenty minutes with common tools is a “weapon” that “may readily be converted” to fire under 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(3)(A), so ATF’s 2022 rule reaching such kits is valid in at least some applications and survives a facial challenge; harder kits were left for later cases.

sections.Parties: The petitioners were the Attorney General (Bondi, substituted for Garland) and the federal officials responsible for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, defending ATF’s 2022 rule. The respondents were individual gun owners, at-home gunsmiths, firearm manufacturers and dealers, and allied organizations that brought a pre-enforcement challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act. Justice Gorsuch wrote for a seven-Justice majority on March 26, 2025; Justice Jackson concurred; Justice Thomas dissented, as did Justice Alito.
sections.Material Facts: Congress enacted the Gun Control Act of 1968 after finding that criminals could too easily obtain untraceable guns. Section 921(a)(3)(A) defines a firearm to include “any weapon (including a starter gun) which will or is designed to or may readily be converted to expel a projectile by the action of an explosive.” Sellers treated kits as outside the Act; “ghost guns” submitted for tracing rose from about 1,600 in 2017 to more than 19,000 in 2021. ATF’s 2022 rule read the definition to cover a kit designed to, or readily capable of being completed, assembled or converted to, expel a projectile. Kits vary widely: some omit essential parts and demand specialized skill, while Polymer80’s “Buy Build Shoot” kit contained every component of a Glock-variant pistol and, in an ATF test, a novice built a working gun in twenty-one minutes with common tools and YouTube instructions.
sections.Procedural History: Before enforcement began the respondents filed what they called a facial challenge under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(C), arguing that the Act categorically excludes weapon parts kits so that the kit provision exceeded ATF’s authority. The Northern District of Texas agreed on summary judgment and vacated the rule, 680 F. Supp. 3d 741 (2023), and the Fifth Circuit largely affirmed, holding that no kit could ever satisfy the statutory definition regardless of completeness or ease of assembly, 86 F.4th 179. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on October 8, 2024, and reversed and remanded. Because the respondents never disputed the government’s account of their facial burden, one valid application of the rule was enough to defeat the challenge.
sections.Issue: Does § 921(a)(3)(A) authorize ATF to regulate at least some weapon parts kits as a “weapon” that “may readily be converted” to expel a projectile, defeating the respondents’ facial claim that ATF lacks authority over every kit? That breaks into whether an unassembled kit can be a weapon at all, whether such a kit may readily be converted to fire, and whether lenity or constitutional avoidance narrows the definition because the Act carries criminal penalties.
sections.Holding: Yes. The definition has two requirements, a “weapon” and one of three functional conditions, and some kits satisfy both. The Polymer80 kit is a weapon because its intended function as an instrument of combat is obvious even before assembly, and it may readily be converted to fire because finishing it takes no more time, effort, expertise or specialized tools than converting a starter gun, which the statute itself treats as a weapon. Since the respondents argued only that no kit could ever qualify, showing that some do defeats the facial challenge. Text, context and structure resolved the examples before the Court, so lenity and avoidance played no role; the classification of more incomplete or labor-intensive kits was reserved. Reversed and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: But “weapon” is an artifact noun, one whose application follows the object’s intended human function, and ordinary speakers use such nouns for unfinished objects when the function is clear: an author’s unfinished novel, a boxed IKEA table awaiting assembly, a rifle disassembled for cleaning. Polymer80 supplied every necessary component, required about twenty minutes of ordinary work, and sold the product as “Buy Build Shoot”; its name says it all. Congress expressly included starter guns, which fire only blanks as sold and can be converted to live fire with a common power tool in under an hour. The starter gun also supplied the yardstick for “readily”: its conversion takes common tools, ordinary skill and less than an hour, and the Polymer80 kit demanded no more. A kit missing essential parts or requiring substantial time, specialized skill or uncommon equipment may fall outside both terms and could support as-applied challenges. Justice Thomas read “weapon” to require an existing instrument usable in combat, distinguished kits from disassembled rifles and starter guns because those have functional frames or receivers, and would have applied lenity to any ambiguity.

lrs-k-cargill.summary: A semiautomatic rifle fitted with a bump stock is not a “machinegun” under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(b): each round follows a separate function of the trigger, which must release and reset between shots, and continued fire depends on the shooter’s sustained forward pressure rather than occurring automatically, so ATF’s 2018 rule exceeded its statutory authority.

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Attorney General Merrick Garland and the federal officials responsible for ATF, defending the agency’s 2018 bump-stock rule. The respondent was Michael Cargill, who owned two bump stocks, surrendered them under protest, and sued under the Administrative Procedure Act. Justice Thomas wrote for a 6–3 Court on June 14, 2024; Justice Alito concurred; Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson.
sections.Material Facts: The National Firearms Act of 1934 defines a machinegun as a weapon that “shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot, automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.” Bump firing uses recoil to speed that cycle: the shooter holds the trigger finger stationary and pushes the rifle forward, so recoil releases the trigger and forward pressure bumps it back into the finger. A bump stock replaces the rifle’s rear stock with a sliding casing and a ledge for the trigger finger. On more than ten occasions ATF had concluded that bump-stock rifles were not machineguns. After a gunman using bump-stock rifles killed fifty-eight people at a Las Vegas festival in October 2017, bills to ban the devices stalled, and ATF reversed course in a 2018 rule that required owners to destroy or surrender the devices within ninety days.
sections.Procedural History: Cargill surrendered two bump stocks under protest and sued under the APA, alleging that ATF exceeded its statutory authority because the devices fall outside § 5845(b). After a bench trial the Western District of Texas entered judgment for ATF, 502 F. Supp. 3d 1163, and a Fifth Circuit panel affirmed, 20 F.4th 1004. On rehearing en banc the Fifth Circuit reversed, 57 F.4th 447: a majority found the statute at least ambiguous and applied the rule of lenity for Cargill, while an eight-judge plurality read it as unambiguously excluding bump-stock rifles. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve a circuit split, heard argument on February 28, 2024, and affirmed.
sections.Issue: Does a bump stock convert a semiautomatic rifle into a “machinegun” under § 5845(b) by enabling it to shoot automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger? The answer turns on two phrases: whether each shot from a bump-stock rifle results from a separate “function of the trigger,” and whether the weapon fires “automatically” when the shooter must keep the right forward pressure on the front grip with the nontrigger hand.
sections.Holding: No, on both grounds. A bump-stock-equipped semiautomatic rifle does not fire more than one shot by a single function of the trigger, because the trigger must release and reset between shots and each bump of the trigger against the stationary finger is a separate function; the bump stock only shortens the time between functions. Even if it fired more than one shot per function, it would not do so automatically, because the shooter must supply continuing manual input by maintaining forward pressure on the front grip, a single function of the trigger “and then some.” ATF therefore exceeded its statutory authority, and the en banc Fifth Circuit’s judgment for Cargill was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Contemporary dictionaries defined “function” as the mode of action by which a thing fulfills its purpose and “trigger” as the lever that activates a mechanism, so “function of the trigger” is the physical trigger movement that fires the weapon. Diagrams of the AR-15’s trigger, hammer and disconnector showed that one engagement fires one cartridge; a later shot requires a new engagement, with or without a bump stock. ATF’s own definition undercut it: the rule defined a function as a pull “and analogous motions,” and ATF conceded that sliding the rifle forward to bump the trigger is such a motion, so each bump is its own function. On “automatically,” the syntax requires the single trigger function itself to cause more than one shot, but bump fire also requires the nontrigger hand to maintain calibrated forward pressure. ATF’s treatment of the Ithaca Model 37 shotgun confirmed the line: holding its trigger while pumping produces multiple shots, yet ATF classifies it outside the definition because the pump supplies manual input. The presumption against ineffectiveness failed because the statute still reaches traditional machineguns.

lrs-k-cargill.separateOpinions: Justice Alito concurred: an M16 and a bump-stock rifle differ little in practice, but the text compels different treatment, and the remedy is legislation, which might already have passed had ATF kept its earlier reading. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, read “single function of the trigger” from the shooter’s perspective as the single human act that starts a firing sequence, relying on 1934 hearing testimony and committee reports equating the phrase with a single pull; a bump-stock shooter initiates fire once and then maintains forward pressure just as an M16 shooter holds the trigger back, and the presumption against ineffectiveness applies because bump stocks fire 400 to 800 rounds a minute.
